analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or raising prices based on genetic information or genetic test use.
analysis.headline: Despite a Republican lead sponsor and 26 cosponsors from both parties, the bill sat in the Senate labor committee for two years, got one hearing in May 1998, and never came to a vote before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for health insurers to deny, cancel, or price coverage based on a person's genetic information or family history, or because they got a genetic test or counseling. It also would have barred insurers from demanding genetic information and from sharing it without written permission, and let people sue for damages if an insurer violated the rules. The protections covered employer plans, individual-market insurance, and Medicare supplement (Medigap) policies.
analysis.who_benefits: People who carry genes linked to diseases like breast cancer, Huntington's, or inherited heart conditions — and their family members. Under the bill, they could learn their genetic risk, get tested, and seek treatment without fear that an insurer would deny them coverage, cancel their policy, or charge them unaffordable premiums. Everyone buying insurance in the individual market or through an employer would have gained a federal privacy right over their genetic information.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and insurers from denying, canceling, refusing to renew, or varying the premiums or terms of coverage based on genetic information or because someone requested or received genetic services, across ERISA plans, the Public Health Service Act framework, and the tax code.
Extends the same ban to the individual insurance market and to issuers of Medicare supplemental (Medigap) policies, so people buying coverage on their own or as seniors are protected too.
Bars plans and insurers from requesting or requiring genetic information about applicants or enrollees, and from disclosing it without prior written authorization for each disclosure.
Gives individuals a right to sue in court for compensatory, consequential, and punitive damages when an insurer violates the protections, adding real enforcement teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer plans, which would lose the ability to use genetic information in deciding who to cover and what to charge. To the extent the rules spread the cost of care for people with genetic risks across the whole risk pool, other premium payers could see modestly higher premiums.

drawbacks.text: By barring insurers from pricing genetic risk, the bill shifts expected costs for people with serious inherited conditions onto the broader insurance pool, which insurers and some employers argued would nudge premiums up for everyone in a group plan.
The bill only covers health insurance. It does nothing about genetic discrimination in employment — hiring, firing, or promotion — a gap that left people with genetic risk exposed on the job side.
Enforcement depends on individuals filing civil lawsuits, and damages are awarded at the court's discretion, so a person wronged by an insurer would have to bear the burden of litigating.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it removes a fear — that getting a genetic test could cost you your coverage — that was already chilling medical decisions at the dawn of genetic medicine. The main cost is a modest redistribution of risk across premium payers, which is the normal trade-off of any anti-discrimination rule in insurance. The bill's genuine weaknesses are its silence on employment discrimination and its lawsuit-only enforcement; neither is a reason to kill it, but both left the protection less complete than it could have been.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's labor committee held a hearing on the bill but never voted to send it to the floor, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Olympia Snowe, a Republican from Maine, introduced the bill on January 21, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
Twenty-six senators signed on as cosponsors — 21 Democrats and 5 Republicans — giving the bill bipartisan support from the start.
The committee held hearings on the bill on May 21, 1998, more than a year after introduction.
No markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill's action history ends with that hearing; the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers came out ahead: without a law, they kept the ability to collect genetic information and use it to deny, cancel, or price coverage. People with genetic disease risk stayed exposed, and the issue was left for a later Congress.

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Jim Jeffords, R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in January 1997, held one hearing in May 1998, and never reported it out for a Senate vote.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on using genetic and health information in insurance underwriting.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by 26 senators of both parties — 21 Democrats and 5 Republicans — so its death in committee was not a party-line vote but a failure to advance at all.

industries.note: The bill strips insurers of their ability to deny, cancel, or reprice coverage based on genetic information or family history, and bars them from demanding or sharing genetic data without written consent. Insurers had used such information in underwriting to keep expected high-cost people out of their pools, a practice that directly cost individuals their coverage.

ERISA-covered plans would face new federal restrictions on collecting genetic information and new liability for violations, but also gain protection against being saddled with adverse selection if competitors' plans screened out genetic risk.

By banning discrimination based on requesting or receiving genetic services, the bill removes a deterrent that kept at-risk people from getting tested, expanding demand for genetic medicine while protecting patients.
